outline.chapter_title: 1. The Dispute and the Statutory Setting
outline.description: This chapter introduces the parties, the factual dispute over AFL’s FOIA request to the Department of Justice, and the statutory framework governing the Office of Special Counsel. It explains why AFL turned to OSC in addition to pursuing its ordinary FOIA suit, and it situates the case within the interaction between FOIA and the Civil Service Reform Act.
subtopics: America First Legal Foundation’s effort to obtain DOJ emails concerning judicial recusals
DOJ’s alleged policy of not searching employee emails without the employee’s consent
AFL’s two-track strategy: a direct FOIA suit against DOJ and a separate effort to trigger OSC investigation
The role of the Office of Special Counsel as an investigative and prosecutorial civil-service agency
OSC authority under 5 U.S.C. § 1214 to investigate prohibited personnel practices and seek corrective or disciplinary action
OSC authority under 5 U.S.C. § 1216 to investigate other misconduct, including arbitrary or capricious FOIA withholdings
FOIA’s separate OSC-related enforcement provision in 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(4)(F)(i)
Why the apparent overlap between § 1216 and § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) created the legal controversy

outline.chapter_title: 2. Procedural History and the District Court’s Merits Ruling
outline.description: This chapter traces how the case reached the D.C. Circuit. It explains OSC’s refusal to investigate, the district court’s partial agreement with AFL on statutory interpretation, its refusal to compel an investigation, the remand to OSC, and the final dismissal that produced the appeal.
subtopics: AFL’s request that OSC investigate DOJ under § 1216(a)(3)
OSC’s position that it lacked authority absent the three FOIA-specific predicates in § 552(a)(4)(F)(i)
AFL’s argument that § 1216 independently required an investigation even when § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) was not triggered
The district court’s conclusion that § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) does not limit OSC’s investigative power under § 1216
The district court’s determination that OSC’s refusal rested on legal error
The district court’s further conclusion that, under § 1216(c), whether to investigate a FOIA policy was committed to OSC’s discretion
The remand to OSC for reconsideration rather than an order compelling investigation
OSC’s renewed refusal to investigate and AFL’s motion for entry of final judgment
The appeal to the D.C. Circuit and the court’s de novo review
Why the court of appeals addressed standing before the merits despite the district court’s merits-based disposition

outline.chapter_title: 3. Article III Standing and the Court’s Procedural-Injury Framework
outline.description: This chapter develops the constitutional threshold issue that ultimately decided the case. It explains the standing requirements, the court’s reliance on supplemental briefing, and the doctrinal distinction between a bare procedural violation and a procedural violation tied to a concrete interest.
subtopics: Article III’s case-or-controversy requirement as the source of standing doctrine
The three familiar standing elements: injury in fact, causation, and redressability
The pleading burden at the motion-to-dismiss stage
Why federal courts must examine standing before reaching the merits
AFL’s theory that OSC violated a statutory procedural right to an investigation under § 1216
The rule from Summers v. Earth Island Institute that a procedural right in the abstract is insufficient
The D.C. Circuit’s relaxed standing approach for procedural-rights cases
What remains required even under the relaxed standard: a concrete, particularized interest and adequate causation
The court’s choice not to classify AFL’s asserted injuries as definitively procedural or substantive because standing failed even under the more forgiving procedural-injury framework
How the standing inquiry reframed the case away from statutory entitlement and toward constitutional justiciability

outline.chapter_title: 4. Why AFL’s Two Standing Theories Failed
outline.description: This chapter is the analytical core of the opinion. It separately examines the two injuries AFL asserted and shows why the court found each one insufficient. The chapter highlights the court’s emphasis on speculative causal chains, independent actors, enforcement discretion, and the limits of informational standing.
subtopics: AFL’s first theory: OSC’s failure to investigate prevented AFL from obtaining the FOIA records it sought from DOJ
Why the court treated any immediate informational injury regarding records as traceable to DOJ rather than OSC
The speculative causal chain identified by the court: OSC investigation, possible OSC enforcement action, possible MSPB sanction, and possible DOJ production
The significance of independent actors not before the court, especially MSPB and DOJ
The court’s use of FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine on speculation about third-party choices
The court’s invocation of Heckler v. Chaney and the problem of agency enforcement discretion
Why a favorable judgment would not 'very likely' redress AFL’s inability to obtain records
The court’s reliance on Haaland v. Brackeen to stress that redressability generally depends on relief binding the parties, not persuasive effect on outsiders
AFL’s second theory: OSC’s refusal to investigate deprived AFL of notices and information associated with an OSC investigation
The doctrine of informational standing: denial of information that a statute entitles the plaintiff to receive
Why § 1216(a)(3), even if mandatory as to investigation, does not itself create an entitlement to information
AFL’s attempt to rely on § 1214 notice provisions through § 1216 investigations
Why that argument failed because AFL did not contend that § 1214 notice requirements must apply in § 1216 investigations
The importance of Carson v. Office of Special Counsel and the discretionary nature of using § 1214 procedures in a § 1216 investigation
Why the absence of a statutory entitlement defeated concrete injury and also undermined redressability for the second theory

outline.chapter_title: 5. Holding, Disposition, and the Opinion’s Significance
outline.description: This chapter explains the formal outcome and the opinion’s practical importance. It clarifies what the court did and did not decide, how the jurisdictional ruling erased the district court’s merits judgment, and what the case teaches about suits seeking to compel government investigations.
subtopics: The court’s holding that AFL lacked Article III standing
The resulting disposition: vacatur of the district court’s judgment and remand with instructions to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction
Why a lack of standing prevented the D.C. Circuit from resolving the underlying statutory merits question
What remains undecided about the relationship between § 1216 and FOIA’s § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) enforcement provision
The difference between a favorable statutory argument and a justiciable federal case
The case as an example of the limits on suits seeking to force agency investigation or enforcement activity
The opinion’s treatment of informational injury as requiring a concrete statutory entitlement to receive information
The broader lesson on causation and redressability when relief depends on multiple discretionary acts by third parties
How the case fits within modern standing doctrine in the D.C. Circuit and Supreme Court precedent
